meta.title: Hindi A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hindi → English (see the Hindi, recall the meaning) and English → Hindi (see an English meaning, recall the Hindi). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hindi, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 281 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, postpositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 219 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hindi, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Devanagari with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ā ī ū for the long vowels, a tilde or a dot for nasalisation: khānā, ma͠i), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Hindi Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. The 214 nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, which every adjective, postposition and past-tense verb agrees with, and their plural; the 77 verbs show their past forms, where Hindi verbs are irregular, and behind the All forms fold their present, future, subjunctive and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 493 of the 500 words, three apiece for 471 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
